Each top node in turn is joined to the bottom nodes with the most degree left, the fewest, or alternately the most and the fewest, so the three variants wire the same six edges differently while every node still meets its pill and no pair is joined twice." width="100%"} Creates `len(aseq)` nodes in a first part and `len(bseq)` in a second, and gives first-part node `i` exactly `aseq[i]` neighbors and second-part node `j` exactly `bseq[j]`, with no parallel edges. The construction repeatedly takes the first-part node with the most degree left, say `d`, and joins it to `d` second-part nodes, chosen by `variant=`: - `"largest"` (default): the `d` nodes with the most degree left. This succeeds whenever any simple bipartite graph has these degrees (the Gale-Ryser condition), and is NetworkX's `bipartite.havel_hakimi_graph()` - `"smallest"`: the `d` nodes with the least degree left, in their initial order, as in NetworkX's `bipartite.reverse_havel_hakimi_graph()` - `"alternating"`: alternately one of the largest and one of the smallest, as in NetworkX's `bipartite.alternating_havel_hakimi_graph()` The variants spread the edges differently: `"largest"` concentrates them among the high-degree nodes (strongly assortative), `"smallest"` pairs hubs with low-degree nodes (disassortative), and `"alternating"` lands in between. The `"smallest"` and `"alternating"` choices can paint themselves into a corner and fail on sequences that `"largest"` realizes. NetworkX then silently returns a graph with the wrong degrees or with parallel edges, and it also counts second-part nodes of degree `0` as targets; here the graph is always simple with every degree exact, and a construction that can't finish raises `ValueError`. Each node's part is stored in the `part_attr=` node attribute (`0` for the first, `1` for the second). The first part is created first, and in a directed graph every edge points from the first part to the second. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Bipartite Havel-Hakimi graphs are useful for: - checking that a pair of degree sequences can be realized by a bipartite graph, and getting one realization - deterministic starting points for degree-preserving rewiring of two-mode networks - test graphs with exactly prescribed degrees and a controlled degree mixing ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [aseq]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Degrees of the first-part nodes, as a list of non-negative integers. [bseq]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Degrees of the second-part nodes, as a list of non-negative integers. Must have the same sum as `aseq=`. [variant]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["largest"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Which second-part nodes each step joins: `"largest"` (default), `"smallest"` or `"alternating"`. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. Default is `"part"`. Pass `None` to skip storing it. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a degree is negative, the two sequences have different sums, `variant=` is not one of the three names, or the construction runs out of second-part nodes (for `"largest"`, exactly when no simple bipartite graph has these degrees). ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Each node gets the degree at its position, first part then second: ::: {#32b4d2b4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_bipartite_havel_hakimi_graph([3, 2, 1], [2, 2, 1, 1]) [graph.get_degree(v) for v in sorted(graph.get_node_ids())] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [3, 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 1] ``` ::: ::: The variants realize the same degrees with different edges. With `"largest"` the first-part hub `"1"` takes both second-part nodes of degree `2`, `"4"` and `"5"`; with `"smallest"` it starts with `"6"` and `"7"`, of degree `1`: ::: {#497355d9 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} for variant in ("largest", "smallest", "alternating"): g = ec.Graph().add_bipartite_havel_hakimi_graph([3, 2, 1], [2, 2, 1, 1], variant=variant) print(variant, g.get_edges_str_repr()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` largest ['1--7', '1--4', '1--5', '2--5', '2--6', '3--4'] smallest ['1--6', '1--7', '1--4', '2--4', '2--5', '3--5'] alternating ['1--4', '1--6', '1--5', '2--7', '2--4', '3--5'] ``` ::: ::: One first-part node can't have three neighbors when the other side has only two nodes: ::: {#8216d9a5 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} try: ec.Graph().add_bipartite_havel_hakimi_graph([3, 1], [2, 2]) except ValueError as err: print(err) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` the degree sequences can't be realized by this construction: node 0 needs 3 neighbors but only 2 nodes of the other part have degree left ``` ::: :::
